#740. Australian Consumer Advocacy Group Blasts Ticketing Giants for ‘Fleecing Fans’

Reps for Ticketmaster and Ticketek have responded.

Ticketek and Ticketmaster have collected Choice’s Shonky Awards, a dubious honor handed out to those businesses deemed to offer some of the nation’s worst products and services.

The ticketing giants were responsible for “fleecing fans,” remarks Choice CEO Monique Perry, as the consumer advocacy group on Wednesday (Nov. 4) announced its 2026 Shonkys. Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

The ticketing companies were fingered for “gouging consumers during a cost-of-living crisis,” reads a statement issued by Choice. “Both companies have used a number of sneaky tactics, like dynamic pricing or ‘in demand’ tickets, to push ticket prices for live events to ridiculous new heights.”

Time and time again, Perry continues, the ticketing companies have used “sneaky tactics such as dynamic pricing or higher-cost ‘in demand’ tickets, concealing ticket prices ahead of sale and strict time limits to take advantage of fans desperately wanting to secure a spot. We think that’s pretty shonky.”

In one example provided by the not-for-profit organization, John Farnham fans who logged on to Ticketek to secure tickets to a tribute concert were faced with inflated prices of up to A$1,650 ($1,153).

Reps for Ticketmaster and Ticketek have responded.

“Ticketmaster is committed to giving fans a safe, secure and transparent way to buy tickets to thousands of events each year. We continually invest in technology to protect fans, improve the ticket-buying experience, and make ticketing more transparent across our platform,” reads a statement issued to Billboard from the ticketing giant, part of Live Nation. Ticket prices are set by event organizers, not Ticketmaster, the message continues. “We do not use surge pricing or algorithms that automatically increase prices in response to real-time demand.”

And for “in demand tickets,” event organizers set the prices of hot tickets “closer to market value and may review these over the sales period. These prices do not automatically increase because more fans join a queue,” the Ticketmaster statement reads.

“We’re committed to helping fans understand how ticketing works and providing clear information about ticket pricing and their options.”

A spokesperson for Ticketek, part of the TEG, disputed the claims concerning the John Farnham tribute, noting the premium ticket, Ultimate, priced at A$1,650, was not affected by dynamic pricing. “Ultimate is a ring-fenced premium ticket and the pricing did not change for this category for this event,” reads a statement from Ticketek. “Ultimate tickets made up less than one per cent of the tickets available for the event.”

Where variable pricing was used for the event, billed as The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend – The Celebration Concert, fewer than 7% of tickets were affected, which meant that for most ticket categories, prices didn’t budge, according to reps. Where they did, around 3.7 per cent of tickets were in categories where the price increased, while 3.3% were in categories where the price decreased, while upwards of 92% of tickets were sold at their original, unchanged fixed price.

Ticketek reiterated that ticket prices are set by the artist, promoter or event organizer, and variable pricing is only used when they choose to — in which case, consumers are notified about potential price changes before they enter the on-sale. “The vast majority of tickets sold through Ticketek are checked out at a price set before the on-sale opens,” reads the statement.

Choice keeps close tabs on the ticketing industry. The group has campaigned for a cleaner, clearer secondary ticketing market and, as part of that crusade, bestowed a “Shonky” to Viagogo in 2017, citing “dodgy practices that tick off consumers.”

An independent, nonprofit member organization since 1959, Choice put a string of businesses and industries on blast this year, including Virgin Australia, Hisense, Petcover, Quest Protein Chips and Sony Interactive Entertainment.

The Shonkys are now in their 21st year. Read more here.

Can you see the "cat's head" in this nebula?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This "cat's head" would work perfectly in a witch's cauldron, glowing red "eyes" and all.

Just in time for Halloween, we have new, ghostly views of the Cat's Eye Nebula haunting the outer reaches of the cosmos.

This nebula earned its name from its distinctive "cat's head" shape, which you can see on the left-hand side of these two images snapped by both the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes. In these new images, you can even see the cat's glowing red "eye," which experts suggest could be a young star trapped in the nebula's dusty clutches.

Found about 7,500 light-years away from Earth, this star-forming region can be found within the larger Carina Nebula.

As the stars in the Carina Nebula continue to form, grow and evolve over time, the Nebula itself will change and eventually, this "cat's head" won't look much like a cat anymore. But for now, we can enjoy this vision of a domestic cat somehow depicted in this colossal tour of gas and dust.

As a special Halloween treat, we have not one, but three new images of the cosmic cat's head.

In the snapshot captured by Hubble, we can see the nebula in visible light. This view shows the nebula as a brown pillar of dust embedded in a hazy, almost rainbow field of dust and gas. These colors are captured through Hubble's filters that can see the light coming from oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur and the light scattered by nebula dust.

JWST also took a look at this cat's head, observing the nebula in near- and mid-infrared wavelengths.

By looking at the same objects in space through different wavelengths and with different instruments and telescopes, we can uncover completely new and different details about these far-off celestial objects.

Nature reported in June on a survey that shows how poor supervision can drive early-career researchers out of academia (see Nature 654, 304–305; 2026). As a newly appointed supervisor of master’s students at a Chinese university, I have begun to confront this issue from the other side of the power dynamic. The LLRV was a bizarre, four-legged flying contraption commonly known as the "Flying Bedstead" used by Apollo astronauts for moon landing practice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On October 30, 1964, NASA's Lunar Landing Research Vehicle, or LLRV, took to the skies for the first time.

The LLRV was a bizarre, four-legged flying contraption commonly known as the "Flying Bedstead." NASA used it to simulate moon landings and liftoffs on Earth to prepare for Apollo 11, the first crewed lunar landing.

The first person to give it a whirl was the X-15 pilot Joe Walker. During this test flight, he reached an altitude of about 10 feet, and he hovered there for about a minute. He did this two more times that same day. In all, he completed more than 30 test flights with the LLRV.

These test flights took place at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. That facility has since been renamed the Armstrong Flight Research Center after Neil Armstrong, who also piloted — and famously crashed — the "Flying Bedstead" before he went to the moon.

Over 60 years ago this LLRV test flight was a critical step toward landing humans on the moon for the first time, a historic moment that both served an important political purpose while also showcasing the result of monumental scientific and technical progress.

While images from this test flight might look like the team are having a bit of fun out in the desert, and perhaps they were, it was also deadly serious. The astronauts who signed onto these crewed missions were doing something that had never been attempted. They were putting their lives on the line for this progress, and this testing was a major piece in reassuring them and NASA that lunar landing could be accomplished, and safely.

Today, as we return humans to the moon with NASA's Artemis program, we see parallels between testing done over 60 years ago and testing today. Right now, SpaceX and Blue Origin are testing their lunar landers for crewed lunar landings in the near-future. While we have now been to the moon and have safely and successfully landed humans before, these tests remain critical for the safety and success of the missions.

#735. Trumper’s Remorse: Voters Look at the Last Two Years and Ask for a Redo

With a crushing Democratic rout in both the House and Senate, America seems to want to Replayola everything that's happened since 2024.

Even the most forgiving retailers tend to cap a return policy at 90 days. Show up after that, you’re out of luck. But voters across America on Tuesday took a look at what they purchased two Novembers ago and said: “How about 730 days, would you accept that? The merchandise is a little battered, but the tags are intact.”After months of political fighting both substantive and surreal, with debates over ideology and reflections on buttocks, American voters Tuesday delivered as strong a rebuff to a Republican president as has been delivered in four decades, turning the House of Representatives and Senate over to Democrats and essentially saying “you see if you can stop him.”Democrats won in swing states and they won in red states; they won in states where Trump had been ascendant and states where Republicans never gave up control. They won with moderates and they won with firebrands. They won, improbably, in rural counties all over the country.From Maine to Texas, Kansas to South Carolina — heck, as of this writing even Mississippi was in play — new Democratic Senators were springing up everywhere. They won so often cable news pundits ran out of water puns for their blue-wave metaphor. They won so much, they may have even gotten tired of winning.Democrats gained, as of this writing, a whopping 41 seats in the House, far more than the three needed to win control. But it was the Senate — where a flip was far from assured and in fact unlikely just weeks ago — where the most drama abided.The four-seat requirement was met. Then it became five. Then six. States where Democrats hadn’t won a Senate seat in 38 years (Texas) or in 94 years (Kansas). States where Trump two years ago won by double digits (Ohio) and states where Strom Thurmond presided for half a century (South Carolina).And even, it turned out, in a state where Democrats hadn’t beaten a Susan Collins in 30 years (Maine).As of this writing, Democrats had flipped seven Senate seats with an eye on an eighth in Alaska and a ninth in Mississippi, using every last vote of that 43-vote lead. They were also holding on to all their blue seats, including Michigan, called by CNN for Abdul El-Sayed at 2:30 am local time.There have been major Congressional shifts like his before, most notably in 1994 for Republicans and 2008 for Democrats. But both of those quakes occurred because of a galvanizing candidate in the winning party — Newt Gingrich in 1994 and Barack Obama in 2008. What was remarkable about this sweep is that it didn’t come from one central charismatic figure but a slew of grassroots personalities who understood their individual constituencies, state-by-state: James Talarico and Josh Turek and Annie Andrews and Adam Hamilton. (Also, speaking of Talarico and Hamilton, it’s nice Democrats finally figured out what the Republicans did decades ago: overtly Christian candidates play.)And, of course, the Trump remorse. Because there was a political figure who mobilized the electorate — just in the negative. How fittingly 2026 that the candidate who influenced voters most was the one people liked least, Donald Trump, with his policies on ICE and Iran, with his DOGE slashings and science evisceratings and health-care-benefit reducing and the fact that prices still seem to be going up while the only thing that seems to be coming down is the East Wing. “American people are hurting,” Van Jones said on CNN, boiling it to the quick, “and this dude’s out of touch.”Perhaps the best modern comp to all this is 1986. That Election Day, 40 years ago, Democrats scored big in the midterms — also in the second term of a fading Republican giant, netting eight seats during the presidency of Ronald Reagan.This election season has been one of the most entertaining, if also the most divisive, in recent memory as a showman president distrusted even by many of his own party paved the way to a series of colorful and ultimately losing showdowns.Books can be written about all the dynamics, but fights over Middle East policy of course roiled and at times threatened to break apart the Democratic party — right up until the final days with Haley Stevens’ shocking defection in Michigan. And yet somehow it all led to history — the first openly gay male senator in New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas, the first Black female governor in Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms.Meanwhile, Republicans tried to look toward the future while grappling with the Donald Trump present, accepting his campaign appearances even as they kept him out of nearly all of their ads. (Democrats, on the other hand, were all too happy to tether their opponents to the president.)And through it all the president himself, getting distracted with boasts and random talk as he hit the hustings of a trail where he was only ambivalently wanted.The Democrats will face mountains ahead, not least thanks to the schisms in their own party; how will the Darializa Chevalier and Melat Kiros types in the House play with the mainstream types led by new speaker Hakeem Jeffries (the first Black Speaker in American history). And, in the Senate, how will Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed meld with moderates like Turek and Hamilton, not to mention Majority Leader Chuck Schumer.The Democrats will also have to decide how much to lean into inquiries and investigations, as this is not what voters sent them to Washington for — it’s the economy, stupid, as James Carville’s whiteboard words continue to redound.But the bigger questions lie with Republicans, who now must decide in the minority how to oppose Democrats — how much to genuflect to a man they have spent much of the past decade paying fealty to, now newly irrelevant. Perhaps the person most confused today, strategically: JD Vance. What or whom exactly is he supposed to be defending, and how does he find a path to the 2028 primaries intact?

But all those questions loom in January. On this November day Democrats really only care about one: “Would you like that as cash or credit?”

#734. Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny

Senegal is hosting Africa's first Youth Olympics, with 2,700 young athletes competing in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. The Games bring pride and hope, but also questions over cost, rights and legacy.

On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports.

Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future.

"I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW.

"I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 Youth Games in Senegal will also be a first beyond the history it is making in Africa.

"Of the 2,700 athletes who will be competing in Dakar, there will be a 50-50 split between men and women," Olivia Nloga, Chief Brand Promotion Officer on the organizing committee, told DW.

"But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists."

Several sports are also making their debut at the Youth Olympic Games, such as five-a-side baseball, kung fu and the Senegalese specialty of beach wrestling. There's also a refugee team at the Youth Olympic Games for the first time.

"As I said earlier, the Youth Olympic Games aren't just about sports, and they aren't just about infrastructure," said Nloga.

"For us, it was also important to use this time to build on and reinforce the idea that these Games in Senegal are a celebration for the people. We did this by investing in culture—for example, through a fashion show and a program called Yi-sol, which is a mural project on the city's walls."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other projects designed to celebrate the people include music, and a local student designed the mascot. The biggest focus of all though, is on creating sustainability for the young people of Senegal.

"We did so through a program that is very important to us – one that is close to our hearts, namely, the Olympic Civic and Sports Certificate," Nloga said.

"We traveled to schools throughout Senegal and worked with more than 1,000 instructors to reach and make an impact on more than one million young Senegalese children who, during this hiatus, were exposed to and educated about the values of the Olympic Movement."

With recent flooding in the country, there were concerns that infrastructure would have been affected, but Nloga insisted that flood risk had long been in the planning.

"The prime minister held an interdepartmental meeting during which he established a task force to ensure that the necessary arrangements and follow-up measures are put in place to safeguard both the competition venues and the accommodation sites."

With Formula 1 confirming its return to Africa earlier in October, global sport is slowly becoming a more regular event in Africa. As a result though, there have been questions asked about the legacy of such events.

Many in Senegal concerned by the high cost of living and unemployment will see these Games as an unnecessary expense. For the Senegalese authorities though, they are an opportunity for long-term investment in the country's young people as well as infrastructure. There is also the hope that this will make Dakar a major tourist destination.

There was further criticism of the Games being in Senegal from Human Rights Watch (HRW), with the NGO calling on the Senegalese authorities to change their stance on the LGBTQ+ community.

"You are welcoming all of the world. It shouldn't be 'you are welcome to our country, except this, except that,'" Larissa Kojoue from HRW told DW.

"Anti-LGBT legislation and that crackdown that is going on, they contradict the Olympic movement, the Olympic Charter, and also various human rights convention that the country has signed."

Earlier this year, Senegal President Bassirou Diomaye Faye signed into law new legislation on same-sex relations that have proved contentious abroad despite broad political support within the majority Muslim country's parliament. Several human rights groups had voiced concerns about the bill, including warning that it would dissuade people at risk of illnesses like HIV/AIDS from seeking help.

The Games were set to see the return of Russians to Olympic competition under their own colours after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted their suspension in July.

However, the Russian Athletics Federation (RusAF) released a statement the day before the opening ceremony saying the reported 13 athletes (and 10 coaches) had been exluded from the competition. They demanded an explanation and asked for the decision to be reconsidered.

"The IOC-endorsed position was clear in its direction: young athletes holding Russian or Belarusian passports should no longer be restricted from international youth competitions. That principle should apply to Dakar 2026," read the statement.

Despite the IOC's ruling, each federation can still decide whether to authorize Russian participation. World Athletics, has clearly upheld their ban, while swimming and judo have allowed Russian athletes back.

"This has enabled World Athletics to pursue its own exclusory agenda in the face of clear and just directions from the IOC. This activism is only detrimental to youth sports, with the result being that Russian young athletes will be denied the opportunity to compete at these Games."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the various concerns, there is an overriding hope that the Games will be prove beneficial for all involved.

"What makes the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar special is that they are also rooted in Senegal's extremely strong sporting culture," Nloga said.

"Every evening, when you take a stroll along the Corniche in Dakar, you're struck by the number of people you see exercising, regardless of their age or physical condition. What we'll be offering during these Olympic Games is also an immersion into Senegalese life – into the way sports are just as much a part of Senegalese identity."

This article was updated on October 30, 2026 to reflect the change in situation for Russian athletes at the Games.

Sira Thierij conducted interviews for this article. Edited by: Chuck Penfold

#733. ‘Beds Are Burning,’ ‘Friday on My Mind’ Among First Songs Inducted Into Australia’s National Songbook

An initiative of APRA AMCOS and NFSA, the project preserves "the songs that have helped shape Australia's cultural identity."

Protest, partying, and observations on the great southern land and its people are among the themes that shine through in Australia’s National Songbook, into which the first batch of songs were inducted on Wednesday (Nov. 4). Explore Midnight Oil See latest videos, charts and news

Announced at a special event at the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia in the nation’s capital, Canberra, 10 songs were elevated into The National Songbook, a new, annual initiative that recognizes the songs, songwriters and composers “whose creative vision has given voice to Australian stories.” Related The Lettermen's Tony Butala Dies at 87 Karol G Sweeps Latin Airplay's Top 3 With 'No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto' Tracks Steve Ellis, Love Affair Singer, Dies at 76

Among the standouts, Midnight Oil’s “Beds Are Burning,” the Easybeats’ “Friday on My Mind,” Helen Reddy’s “I Am Woman,” The Presets’ “My People,” Yothu Yindi’s “Treaty,” and Andrew “Banjo” Paterson’s “Waltzing Matilda.”

Reddy’s “I Am Woman,” which topped the Billboard Hot 100 in December 1972, won a Grammy for best pop vocal performance, female, in 1973 and was voted into the U.S.’ National Recording Registry in 2025. The Easybeats’ “Friday on My Mind” and Midnight Oil’s “Beds Are Burning” both reached the top 20 on the Hot 100, in 1967 and 1988, respectively.

An initiative of APRA AMCOS and NFSA, the project preserves “the songs that have helped shape Australia’s cultural identity,” and launches to coincide with APRA’s 100th anniversary.

“No ten songs could ever tell the whole story of Australia, but together these inaugural inductees help us understand, as a nation, where we’ve come from, who we are and the values we’ve carried through generations,” comments Dean Ormston, CEO of APRA AMCOS.

“As APRA celebrates 100 years of championing songwriters, composers and music publishers, we welcome these debut entries into The National Songbook as songs that have helped become part of our shared cultural story, reflecting the extraordinary breadth, diversity and richness of Australian songwriting and composing.”

As it grows, the songbook will serve as a permanent digital archive, a vault that safeguards music treasures for future generations.

“The National Songbook reflects the remarkable breadth of Australian songwriting and composition, from songs of protest, belonging and identity to works that have become woven into our national story and our DNA,” remarks Meagan Loader, chief curator of the NFSA.

“As Australia’s audiovisual archive, the NFSA will ensure these songs and stories are preserved in our national collection of works of significant cultural heritage, heft and heart, providing a new way for Australians now and into the future to engage with the songs and songwriters who have shaped us.”

The inaugural inductees are said to represent more than a century of Australian storytelling, creativity and cultural expression and are selected by an expert panel.

Stream the National Songbook playlists on Apple Music, Spotify and YouTube Music and visit NFSA for more.

“I Am Woman”Written by Helen Reddy and Ray BurtonReleased: 1971

“My Island Home”Written by Neil MurrayReleased: 1987 (Warumpi Band) 1995 (Christine Anu)

“My People”Written by Julian Hamilton / Kim MoyesReleased: 2007

The Boys soundtrack by The NecksWritten by Chris Abrahams / Tony Buck / Lloyd SwantonReleased: 1998

This has been a pretty rough week for "Star Trek" royalty on this 60th anniversary year with the deaths of both Walter Koenig, "Star Trek's" Lt. Pavel Chekov on Sunday, Oct. 25 and Patrick Stewart, the storied sci-fi property's Captain Jean Luc-Picard on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

With the passing of Walter Koenig at the age of 90 this past week, franchise luminaries of all degrees are coming out with heartfelt condolences, kind words of remembrance, and tearful reflections.

William Shatner, 95, and George Takei, 89, represent the final remaining members of the U.S.S. Enterprise's core crew from "Star Trek: The Original Series" and they both took to social media to express their deep sorrow over losing one of their fellow travelers in the final frontier.

"I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig’s passing," Shatner posted on Instagram.

"Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original 'Star Trek' series and the six films that followed. What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years, was a man who genuinely loved the 'Star Trek' community.

"At conventions, Walter was rarely content to remain behind a signing table. He preferred to be among the people who had kept 'Star Trek' alive for so many decades. That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him.

"My condolences to his family, his friends, and the countless fans whose lives he touched."

George Takei, who portrayed Lt. Hikaru Sulu and co-starred with Koenig on two seasons of "The Original Series" from 1967-69, as well as six subsequent "Star Trek" feature films, offered similar thoughts in memoriam.

"My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," Takei shared on his Instagram page.

"Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date.

"Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too.

"Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

The Taurids produce only a handful of meteors an hour. That sounds disappointing, but I've learned that expecting almost nothing can make this one of the most enjoyable meteor showers of the year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I used to make a basic mistake with meteor showers — I treated the zenith hourly rate (ZHR) like a timetable. If a shower were advertised at 20 meteors per hour, I'd go outside expecting something roughly every three minutes. After 10 quiet minutes, I'd start wondering what I was doing wrong. After half an hour, I'd start to doubt the whole idea of meteor showers.

The Northern and Southern Taurids cured me of all that. Two linked meteor showers that peak around Nov. 4-5 and Nov. 11-12 this year, they each manage only about five meteors per hour under ideal conditions. In reality, you may see fewer. You may spend a long time seeing none. So what's the point?

I've come to regard their paucity of "shooting stars" as a feature, not a flaw, for the Taurids have taught me to stop counting meteors and instead just observe the sky. I go outside for Taurus, the Pleiades, Auriga, and whatever else happens to be visible. If a Taurid crosses the sky, excellent. If not, the evening hasn't failed. The reason is that they are also known for occasionally producing very bright meteors, or fireballs — although "occasionally" is important. Don't go outside expecting a procession of them.

The Taurids hit Earth's atmosphere at about 18 miles (29 kilometers) per second. That's relatively slow for a meteor shower. It's one reason Taurids can be more memorable than meteors from faster showers.

For observers across much of the Northern Hemisphere, Taurus rises in the east during the evening and becomes increasingly well placed as the night progresses. Later evening into the overnight hours is therefore the best time to watch.

I love looking at the night sky around Taurus, but you really don't need to stare at it if you're looking for Taurids. The radiant is indeed within Taurus (close to the Pleiades), but meteors can appear anywhere in the sky. Look roughly east or southeast, then watch as much sky as possible for an hour or so.

This year the moon helps out. The new moon falls on Nov. 9, leaving only a young waxing crescent around the shower's peak. It sets during the evening, giving us properly dark skies later on.

My Taurid observing strategy involves doing little direct meteor observing. I'll likely head outside once Taurus is reasonably high in the eastern sky, probably sometime in the later evening, and give myself other things to look at. The Pleiades are an obvious target — it's exciting to have this little open cluster back in the evening sky. So are the Hyades open cluster and bright orangey Aldebaran, also in Taurus. I'll probably set my smart telescope on the Pleiades and leave it alone to build up a long integration while I spend as much time as I can taking in the whole sky. Meteors are a naked-eye event and demand your attention — the second you avert your gaze from the night sky, a "shooting star" will appear. All stargazers know that!

I won't travel for hours to find perfect darkness. A darker location will reveal fainter meteors, for sure, but the Taurids' occasional bright members can be seen from less-than-perfect skies. A backyard is fine for this one — make travel plans only for August's Perseids and December's Geminids (moon phases allowing).

Nor will I keep score. Meteor rates are statistical descriptions, not promises. Five per hour does not mean one meteor every 12 minutes. You could see two close together and then nothing at all for hours. We're all so used to being told exactly what to expect, but the night sky doesn't work like that — you need to be open to whatever it throws at you (or not). Once you stop expecting the sky to do what you want, meteor showers become more enjoyable.

The moon is moving out of the early evening sky this week, which is exactly what stargazers wait for at this time of year. It reaches third quarter around Nov. 1, rising later at night and leaving the evening dark. That gives us a useful 10-night window for observing before moonlight becomes an issue.

I'm planning to use it for the Andromeda galaxy. From a genuinely dark location, M31 can be spotted with the naked eye as a faint patch. From brighter suburban skies, binoculars make life much easier. The beginner mistake is expecting anything resembling the photographs. Through binoculars, I'm looking for a subtle misty glow, not spiral arms. If you want a more impressive view, get yourself a smart telescope — they do a wonderful job on M31.

There's another practical change this weekend. Daylight saving time ends across most of the U.S. and Canada on Nov. 1. The stars haven't changed their schedule, of course, but getting outside under a dark sky after dinner — and even before — suddenly becomes much easier.

Although you don't need to stare at Taurus, the Bull, to see Taurids, it's an obvious target this week. It's climbing into the eastern sky during the evening. Bright orange star Aldebaran — a red giant 67 light-years from the solar system (and the most luminous star within 100 light-years) — marks the bull's eye. It appears to sit within a V-shape of stars that forms the bull's face. This is the Hyades, the closest open cluster of stars to the solar system at just 150 light-years.

The origin story of both Taurid meteor showers is genuinely awe-inspiring. They're associated with debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke, which orbits the sun once every 3.25 years (1,200 days) — the shortest orbital period of any known comet in the solar system, according to NASA. The second comet ever discovered, Encke, was discovered in 1786 and spans about 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter. It last reached perihelion — its closest point to the sun — on Oct. 22, 2023, and is due to do so again on Feb. 10, 2027, but Earth encounters debris associated with the comet every year.

The picture is more complicated than a single comet trail. The Southern and Northern Taurids are part of the broader Taurid Meteoroid Complex, a vast swarm of interplanetary dust, rocks, comets and asteroids thought to be related to Encke. It's thought that it originates from a much larger object that fragmented as it got close to the sun, perhaps just 5,000 to 6,000 years ago or as much as 20,000 years ago. Fears that huge, mile-wide "planet killer" asteroids may still reside in the Taurid Meteoroid Complex appear to have been ruled out. Phew.

Each fall, Earth passes through different parts of this sprawling stream, producing two overlapping meteor showers — and, occasionally, the larger fragments responsible for the Taurids' famous fireballs.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#728. BAFTA Breakthrough Ted Evans Shares What Sign Language Taught Him About Film – and What’s Next After ‘Retreat’

The British writer-director, featured on the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough list, supported by Netflix, also tells THR how "I always feel I have two audiences" and about his vision for "sign language cinema."

A young woman arrives at a remote wellness retreat for Deaf people, but nothing is what it seems. If you don’t immediately recognize this set-up, you most likely haven’t seen Retreat, the genre-bending debut thriller from British writer-director Ted Evans that has left audiences guessing until the very end.

Billed as “the world’s first deaf thriller” and starring Anne Zander, James Joseph Boyle and Sophie Stone, Retreat, highlighted by THR as a hidden gem, is also a key reason for Evans to feature on the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough list of rising talent, supported by Netflix, which was unveiled on Wednesday. Related Stories Movies 'The Incomer' Attracted Domhnall Gleeson and Moby and Got Its Creator on the BAFTA Breakthrough List. Now, He's Working on a Plan B Film. Movies 'Ish' Has Resonated Widely Amid "Authoritarian Turn," Says Its BAFTA Breakthrough Writer-Director

Among his past work, the creative directed the TV documentary Rose Ayling-Ellis: Signs for Change and short films.

THR talked to Evans about making a splash with his first feature, the short he made with the same title, making the BAFTA Breakthrough list, and what’s next.

Sorry to say that my sign language is not up to snuff. How exciting is it to be a BAFTA Breakthrough creative?Oh, it is a huge honor. It was a big surprise just to be acknowledged and to be amongst these amazing creatives, especially my lead actress, Sophie Stone. To be alongside her for this honor is terrific.How similar is the feature Retreat to your short film that had the same title?It’s a long story. So I made a short film of the same name, and it was about a community. But it was a shoestring short I made for hardly any money at all about 14 years ago. That short did well within the community, but I wasn’t satisfied with it – there was so much more.I then spent a decade excavating and developing something, and it became something completely different thematically. It has the same title, and Sophie was in the short as well, but they’re not really connected. The origin story is much more about us as filmmakers and actors coming together, and the project was born out of that.How cool was it to have a film where all the lead cast members are deaf, and I heard behind the scenes there was also a special focus on the community.Yeah, absolutely. As a deaf man, I grew up in this community, and I’m obviously very passionate about what I call “sign language cinema.” We all have stories ourselves. We’re all part of the human experience, and cinema is such a wonderful way to show the full diversity of what it means to be human. To bring deaf people, our languages, and our culture to cinema has been amazing.We had such an amazing cast, and we did have some deaf talent behind the camera as well. We had sign language directors, assistant directors, and runners and stuff like that. So it was great.And as a filmmaker, working with sign language, which is a visual language, taught me so much more about the medium.Can you share some more insight on that?If you think about continuity, you must make sure that with every shot, every take, there is a flow of continuity. And you think about rhythm and visual grammar. Working with sign language has helped me as a filmmaker understand filmmaking.

I’m not saying that spoken language films don’t [focus on the same things], but you can get away with ADR [Automated Dialogue Replacement], replacing dialogue in post. That is completely different when you’re working with sign language.

What are you hoping for from the BAFTA Breakthrough programs?I have lots of ideas. I write, I direct. I’m looking forward to networking to meet people with a lot more experience and connections in the industry, just to work out the next chapter and what’s possible. Obviously, there are lots of pipe dreams, but you’ve got to be realistic in today’s world. Obviously, it’s not easy. I’m just going to be like a sponge, and I’m just excited to learn really and to make more connections.You mentioned you have a lot of ideas. Is there any new film or series that you’re particularly focused on developing?My slate is quite healthy. I’m allowed to say that I have a horror in development with BBC Film, which is in the very, very early stages. I’m really excited about that. I am hoping to work more inside the community as well as hopefully branch outwards. So, it’s an exciting time.Retreat shows different types of sign languages, but the focus is British Sign Language (BSL). Can people from abroad understand that?Really, American Sign Language is very different from British Sign Language, and actually, more countries are influenced by American Sign Language. In Australia, they have Auslan, which is related to BSL, but they’re all languages of their own. But yes, in fact, in Retreat, we have several languages, including German. If you think about Native American tribes in America, they all had their own languages, but they had an actual sign language that was called Hand Talk, and it was a modality for people to trade between different communities.

What’s your hope for Retreat and its impact?Ultimately, I always feel I have two audiences. I have my community, and then I have the rest of the world. For both of them, number one, you want them to go through a thrilling ride. You want them to enjoy the film, but then there are layers that they can go into.

I hope that it’s universal. I hope it’s not just about our experience. It’s about choice. It’s about understanding what makes you who you are, whether it’s your community or the experience you go through, and what happens when you take one of them out. Hopefully it makes people think. We’re releasing the film early next year into cinemas, which I’m really excited about. We’ve had an amazing year starting at Toronto with our world premiere, and we traveled around the world a lot. So, I just feel really blessed and honored.

#727. Ozzfest 2027 Begins Countdown to … Something

The returning metal fest appears to be gearing up for a major announcement this week.

Fans jacked about the return of Ozzfest may finally have some answers about what the rebooted metal festival will look like on Thursday (Nov. 5). That’s because the hard rock touring event launched by late metal icon Ozzy Osbourne in 1996 started a countdown clock on Tuesday morning that is set to expire at 10 a.m. ET on Thursday morning alongside the caption, “Countdown’s begun.”

At press time no additional information was available on what Thursday’s revelation will be, but Ozzfest has been teasing out the news for the past week, including with a cryptic post featuring the caption “Tell me people…” alongside the iconic O from the Ozzfest logo bisecting a devil’s head. Even more enigmatic was a post over the weekend featuring a sea of white question marks on a black screen.

Ozzy’s widow and longtime manager, Sharon Osbourne, told Billboard earlier this year that she’d been in talks with Live Nation about bringing the festival back next year. “It was something Ozzy was very passionate about: giving young talent a stage in front of a lot of people,” she said. “We really started metal festivals in this country. It was [replicated but] never done with the spirit of what ours was, because ours was a place for new talent. It was like summer camp for kids.” The news was followed a few weeks later by an Ozzfest post that read “Ozzfest could return — 2027?”

The dream then became a reality, with Ozzfest confirming that its reboot will include a stop a Villa Park in Osbourne’s hometown of Birmingham, U.K. next year, as well as the first U.S. dates in nearly a decade. In an Instagram post on Sept. 21, the event announced, “Ozzfest will come to the U.K. and U.S. @theozzfest,” with the caption promising, “More Info Coming Soon!!! Where are you hoping Ozzfest 2027 will pop up?”

And while info is scarce at this moment, fans had plenty of ideas in the countdown post comments, including: “Remaining members of Black Sabbath with Zakk Wylde as lead singer. Black label society opens up!,” “Here we go 🤘 can’t wait to see who’s playing,” “Lineup announcement imminent?,” “Slayer Slayer Slayer” and “Youg Blood headlining.”

Ozzfest was launched by Sharon Osbourne in 1996 after she was unable to book Ozzy on the Lollapalooza festival. Ozzfest then quickly became a popular annual touring festival that brought a day of hard rock and heavy metal to the U.S. and Europe through 2008. Since then, it has taken place on a more sporadic schedule, most recently as a one-day event in 2018 at The Forum in Inglewood, California, with a lineup that featured Rob Zombie, Body Count, Marilyn Manson and others.

Aside from helping lay the foundations for modern rocketry, Jack Parsons performed a bizarre series of ceremonies to try and conjure powerful supernatural entities.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the winter of 1946, two men from very different walks of life walked into California's Mojave Desert together, where one of them became convinced an extraordinary experiment they had been conducting had finally succeeded.

One of the men was pioneering rocket scientist Jack Parsons, a self-taught chemist who helped establish what would become NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and whose innovations in rocket propulsion would help lay the groundwork for the Space Race that would erupt in the years that followed. His unlikely companion was none other than L. Ron Hubbard, then a science fiction writer who had yet to compose the writings that would form the underpinnings of the Church of Scientology that he later established.

Despite Parsons' work with rockets and his companion Hubbard's fictional writings about them, their work together in the early months of 1946 had nothing to do with rocket propulsion, spacecraft, or other technological innovations that would eventually carry humans to space. Instead, Parsons and Hubbard were engaged in an elaborate series of occult ceremonies at the time, whereby they intended to summon an elemental feminine goddess known as "Babalon" (not to be confused with Babylon) to help them bring an otherworldly entity into physical existence.

Their efforts, known today as the "Babalon Working," represent one of the most unusual affairs in American history, with tangential connections to the history of space exploration.

Given its strangeness, the episode has garnered attention from several scholars and historians over the decades, who have sought to understand a series of events at the intersection of science and the occult involving one of the most unconventional innovators behind modern rocket propulsion.

Parsons, born in 1914, would become a key figure in the early development of American rocket technologies by the 1930s and 1940s in California, ultimately helping establish what would become the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). His contributions included the historic experiments at Pasadena's Arroyo Seco on Halloween Day in 1936, which NASA now recognizes as the foundational experiments that launched JPL.

Very much in contrast with his scientific aptitudes, Parsons also cultivated an interest in ceremonial magic during this period. By the early 1940s, he had immersed himself within the California chapter of the Ordo Templi Orientis (OTO), the organization associated with the infamous British occultist Aleister Crowley and his religious philosophy known as Thelema. In 1943, Parsons became the new leader of the organization's Agape Lodge, which subsequently began operating out of his Pasadena residence on South Orange Grove Avenue.

Parsons' occult interests became particularly focused on the evocation of supernatural entities during this period, which the young rocket scientist seemed to genuinely believe could be manifested in the physical world through ritual practices. Ultimately, this led him to undertake an ambitious — and utterly bizarre — series of ceremonies aimed at conjuring what was supposedly one of Thelema's most powerful supernatural entities.

Parsons first became acquainted with L. Ron Hubbard in the summer of 1945, and shortly after meeting, Hubbard became a resident of the scientist's Pasadena home.

While Hubbard had no formal training in the occult arts, Parsons felt he demonstrated the kinds of aptitudes that would make him a promising partner for a serious ceremonial magic undertaking. Thus, in the first days of January 1946, the pair embarked on a series of rituals, which Parsons documented in a manuscript that later became known as The Book of Babalon.

"In the introduction to this text [Parsons] explained that the underlying philosophy for the Babalon Working is that the present age is under the influence of a violent force," noted University of Gothenburg scholar Henrik Bogdan in a 2016 article published in the journal Numen. "The invocation of Babalon was thus, according to Parsons, an attempt to prevent the world from being destroyed."

Specifically, Parsons believed the force of Babalon could be manifested in a specific woman. "In this sense, the Babalon Working was not only an exercise in ritual magic, but a deliberate attempt to bring a divine feminine force into human form," Bogdan notes. With this goal in mind, during the first two weeks of January 1946, the pair worked to invoke this divine feminine figure, associated with liberation and spiritual transformation according to Crowley's Thelemic system.

On January 18, 1946, Parsons and Hubbard traveled into the Mojave Desert, where, according to Parsons' later writings, a change in atmosphere involving their ritual work suddenly became apparent. Now believing their operation had been a success, Parsons declared their work completed, and the two returned to Pasadena.

Soon afterward, Parsons reported to Hubbard that his elemental mistress had seemingly manifested with the sudden appearance at his home of a blue-eyed, red-haired artist named Marjorie Elizabeth Cameron. A former member of the U.S. Navy's WAVES program, Cameron had been invited to Parsons' residence by a colleague who, like Hubbard, was also lodging there at the time. Upon seeing her, Parsons became convinced this was the elemental lover he and Hubbard had worked to conjure, thereby confirming that the Babalon Working had produced its intended result.

Soon, Parsons and Cameron began a relationship, and borrowing ideas from Crowley's 1929 novel Moonchild, Parsons now believed that his romance with Cameron could facilitate the incarnation of a supernatural force through the literal conception of a child using ritual sex magic. The result, Parsons believed, could help to bring about a transformative new dawn in humanity's spiritual development.

This phase of the Babalon Working mainly involved magic rituals and Enochian incantations performed by Parsons and Cameron, with Hubbard present and assisting (in addition to having proposed Rachmaninoff's "Isle of the Dead" as an eerie sonic backdrop for the occasion). For Parsons, the ultimate goal had been to conceive a "magical child" that would become the newborn Thelemic messiah.

Following completion of the rituals in late February 1946, Cameron left on a trip to New York, and Parsons returned to the Mojave Desert where he completed a short treatise entitled Liber 49, believing it to be a "channeled" fourth and final portion of The Book of the Law, Crowley's foundational Thelemic text.

Upon returning from New York, Cameron even claimed to have observed an unusual aerial object—something akin to what later became known as "flying saucers" in the summer of the following year—which she believed to represent the "war engine" referenced in Crowley's work.

Crowley, however, was considerably less enthusiastic about all this. Upon learning what Parsons, Hubbard, and Cameron had been involved with, the famed British occultist confided to a colleague in an April 1946 correspondence that "Apparently he [Parsons] or Ron or somebody is producing a Moonchild. I get fairly frantic when I contemplate the idiocy of these louts."

Ultimately, a growing divide between Crowley and Parsons would cost the rocket scientist his leadership of the Agape Lodge, prompting his departure from Crowley's OTO before the end of 1946. His relationship with Hubbard similarly dissolved due to Parsons' worsening financial situation. Nevertheless, Parsons soldiered on, marrying Cameron in October 1946 and continuing his efforts to usher in a new spiritual age.

On June 17, 1952, Parsons' unusual life ended prematurely when an explosion occurred in his home laboratory, resulting in fatal injuries. He was only 37 years old. Questions still surround the circumstances of his death; while it was ruled an accident, there have been allegations that it was suicide or even a murder.

During his short life, Parsons still managed to make significant contributions to the science of rocket propulsion, securing a place in the history of American space exploration — albeit one that is often overshadowed by the interest historians and scholars have taken in his occult activities.

Nonetheless, Parsons remains a key figure responsible for helping lay the early foundations for what would become America's space program. Although decades before NASA would begin sending its spacecraft in pursuit of answers to cosmic mysteries, one of its early technological pioneers had been seeking answers to such cosmic questions in a very different way: by exploring the boundary between our physical world and the supernatural realms beyond.

Anthony Testa, The Key of the Abyss: Jack Parsons, the Babalon Working and the Black Pilgrimage Decoded (2006), p. 128.

Carter, John. Sex and Rockets: The Occult World of Jack Parsons. New edition. Feral House, 2004.

#725. Russia in Africa: What is Putin hoping to achieve?

Following its invasion of Ukraine and the resulting rift with the West, Russia has declared that it intends to make a "historic return" to Africa. What have we seen of this so far?

The conflict with the West sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine  prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek support from other parts of the world. Africa has become a focus, with foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visiting the continent increasingly often.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has described it as a "historic return," and declared no one and nothing could be compared to what Russia did for Africa in the 20th century.

A Russia-Africa summit has been held in Russia at roughly three-year intervals since 2019. The third takes place in Moscow on October 28 and 29. The program focusses on economic cooperation. Other topics range from politics and security to science and culture. But Russia is actively working with only a few African countries, mainly in the north of the continent, and this is reflected in the trade figures.

"South Africa is still Africa's largest national economy, but its volume of trade with Russia is small, far less than with Egypt and Algeria," says Ivan Klyszcz from the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn, Estonia.

"Egypt and Algeria in particular are key partners for Russia. Egypt plays an important role in this regard. Russian diplomats and business representatives are trying to extend relationships with other countries, especially Tanzania and Ethiopia, but with no appreciable success so far."

Egypt is the second-largest economy in Africa, and the bilateral volume of trade with Russia has more than doubled since 2021; in 2025, according to Russia's Federal Customs Service, it was $10.5 billion (€9.4 billion). Consignments of Russian grain are the main drivers, followed by products of the metal industry. Egypt's exports to Russia are primarily fruit and vegetables.

There are investment projects, too. Russia is building a big nuclear power plant in the Egyptian region of El-Dabaa on the Mediterranean coast. Construction is being financed by a Russian loan of 25 billion US dollars, which covers around 85% of the costs.

Egypt is one of the few African countries with which Russia enjoys stable business relationships, as well as having extensive experience of cooperation, says Nikita Smagin, an expert on Russian policy in the Middle East. "In the long term, Egypt could become Moscow's gateway to Africa and to other markets," he says. "But Cairo is pursuing its own interests. It would be too optimistic to hope that Egypt is lending its support purely out of political solidarity."

According to the Russian customs service, around 39% of Russian–African trade in 2025 was with Egypt, and total sales between Russia and all 54 countries of the African continent came to around 27 billion US dollars. Africa's share of Russia's foreign trade is therefore very small (3.9% in 2025), and not at all commensurate with the attention Moscow is devoting to its relations with African countries.

Russia is not a significant trading partner for Africa, either. The most important partner for African countries is the European Union. In 2025, the volume of trade with the EU came to around 385 billion US dollars. African countries' statistics also show that other partners were well ahead of Russia. The volume of trade with China was in excess of 348 billion US dollars in 2025; with the United States it was almost 105 billion, and 103 billion with India.

Fidel Owusu, a Ghanaian expert with Geopolitical Intelligence Services (GIS) in Liechtenstein, comments that Russia's economic presence in Africa has not been as significant as that of China, the United States, India, or other traditional powers like France and Britain. "If you look at the volume of trade and the kind of investment," he says, "in recent times, some middle powers such as Turkey and the UAW are doing far better than Russia."

Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst with Control Risks, a global risk and strategic intelligence consultancy in Senegal, observes: "Western countries continue to dominate in strategically important areas such as raw material extraction, finance, and the energy sector, even if their political presence in the region is declining." According to her, "Russia will compete more intensively for access to critical mineral resources and energy projects. We see this with lithium projects in Mali as well as with nuclear power initiatives across the continent."

Russia's presence in Africa is more obvious in the military sector than in the fields of trade and investment. Starting with the arrival of the Wagner Group, Russian mercenaries have been supporting African regimes, particularly those of the unstable countries in the Sahel region. In exchange, their associated subsidiaries are granted access to raw materials. Following the death of the Wagner Group leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin, most of these operations were taken over by the Africa Corps, a paramilitary group set up and controlled by Russia's defense ministry.

According to the Congressional Research Service, the think tank of the US Congress, the largest Russian military contingents, each comprising several thousand men, are in the Central African Republic, Mali, and Libya. The Africa Corps is also keen to extend its presence in Burkina Faso and Niger. Russian mercenaries have also been spotted in Equatorial Guinea.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Irina Filatova from the University of Cape Town stresses that there are several reasons why it's important for Russia to maintain a military presence in Africa. "The countries have sizeable deposits of minerals such as gold and uranium. Through them, it's possible to exert influence over Europe's southern borders, including in matters of migration and regional security. With regard to Libya, the country is an important logistical hub for connections with the Sahel and central Africa. Goods can easily be supplied via Libya to countries without access to the sea," Filatova says.

Ultimately, Russia is still one of the biggest suppliers of arms to African countries, even though Russian exports have fallen over the course of the war in Ukraine. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates Moscow's share of the African market for the years 2021–2025 at 15%, which puts it in third place behind the United States (19%) and China (17%). Between 2020 and 2024, its share was even higher: It was in first place with 21%, followed by China with 18%, and the US with 16%.

Ivan Klyszcz from the ICDS says that while Russia is not a significant economic partner for Africa, the fact that it supplies food and fertilizer and has a military presence in some countries means that Moscow's influence in Africa is far greater than is suggested by the volume of trade and investment alone.

"I believe Russia sees the diplomatic weight of Africa," says Fidel Owusu. "When I talk of diplomatic weight, I mean numbers – the continent has the largest number of countries. Russia wants that kind of support in the UN General Assembly whenever votes are cast. In recent times it has done better than in earlier votes."

In recent years, Russia has been positioning itself on the international stage as representing the interests of the Global South.

"We want to work with Africa, we are working with Africa and we will continue to do so. But our aim is not, as it was for the colonial powers, to make money or steal something from Africa, but to develop together," Russian president Vladimir Putin said recently at a conference of the Moscow-based Valdai Discussion Club.

References to the colonial past appeal to some countries but not others, says Irina Filatova. "Africa is not a country, it's a continent. There are differences in the perception of Russia, as well as in the way Russia positions itself. Also, the views of the political elites are often substantially different from those of ordinary citizens. In South Africa, for instance, the Russian narrative is received very positively. An anti-colonial agenda is also popular in other countries, but it isn't necessarily associated with Russia."

Antonio Cascais contributed to this report. It was originally written in Russian.

#724. ‘Ulya’ Director Dives Into His Third Latvian Oscar Contender, Which Stars a Rising Actor as a Female Basketball Legend and Became a “Blockbuster”

Viesturs Kairišs also shares Herzog and Bergman inspirations for the film, opening Tallinn and starring Kārlis Arnolds Avots as Uljana Semjonova, the first non-U.S. woman in the Basketball Hall of Fame.

Latvia made Oscar history in 2025 when Gints Zilbalodis‘ Flow won the best animated feature award. Two years later, the country has selected a very different movie to represent it at the Oscars 2027. The Baltic country picked Ulya from director Viesturs Kairišs (January), which stars up-and-coming Latvian actor Kārlis Arnolds Avots and world-premiered at Cannes in the Un Certain Regard section, as its international best feature film Oscar contender.

Inspired by the life of legendary Latvian basketball player Uljana Semjonova, a two-time Olympic champion and three-time world champion, the black-and-white Ulya follows its protagonist from an isolated rural Old Believer community into the fiercely competitive world of professional basketball. There, she must navigate both the attention drawn by her extraordinary height and the demands of elite sport. Related Stories Movies BAFTA Breakthrough Ted Evans Shares What Sign Language Taught Him About Film - and What's Next After 'Retreat' Movies 'The Incomer' Attracted Domhnall Gleeson and Moby and Got Its Creator on the BAFTA Breakthrough List. Now, He's Working on a Plan B Film.

Semjonova ended up winning the Soviet Union’s national championship and the European Champions Cup 15 times each, the Olympic Gold medal with the USSR in 1976 and 1980, and she became the first non-U.S. woman in the Basketball Hall of Fame.

On Friday, Ulya will open the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF). As a co-production between Latvia, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania, it is also a symbol for the rise of Baltic cinema on the world stage. “Ulya is a very good example of what the Baltic film industries can achieve by working together and with partners beyond our region,” said Triin Tramberg, artistic director of PÖFF. “Our countries may be small, but we have a wealth of stories and creative talent. Co-productions bring those strengths together, help ambitious films reach audiences around the world and give our filmmakers a stronger international presence.”

Avots wrote the script with Livia Ulman and Andris Feldmanis. Wojciech Staroń is the cinematographer, with editing by Armands Zacs. B-Rated International is handling sales for Ulya, produced by Ego Media in Latvia, Allfilm in Estonia, Staroń Film in Poland and Tremora in Lithunia. New Mountain Films has acquired Ulya for North America.

Latvia, which has a population of about 1.8 million, comparable to that of West Virginia, has previously sent two other Kairišs films to the Oscars: his 2022 movie January, a coming-of-age story about an aspiring filmmaker looking to find himself against the backdrop of Latvian independence, and his 2017 film The Chronicles of Melanie, based on the real-life story of a woman who, along with her son, was sent to a labor camp in Siberia in the 1940s after the Soviet occupation of Latvia.

Kairišs talked to THR about Ulya, bringing to life the inner world of a legendary athlete, and how the film, has become a blockbuster in Latvia.

The filmmaker and Avots previously worked together on January. And Kairišs knew that the star was considering writing a play about Semjonova and starring in it. “I heard from Kārlis for a while that his dream was to play Uljana Semjonova,” the director tells THR. When the star told another creative about the idea, “I realized, wow, it’s a film. It’s not a theater play.”

Kairišs didn’t have his eyes on a historical project. “I was a little bit tired of making films connected with Latvian history,” he recalls. “I was not very interested in making something about sports or whatever. But I heard the story about a giant girl living in the deep countryside and then coming to Riga, with the coaches of that time taking her away. And I was seriously touched by this beginning. I immediately had this first image in my head about some far-away environment where a strange tall girl lives, and people suddenly start to look for her.”

Having a male play the female basketball legend was not something he dwelt on. “This was a package. Kārlis is playing Ulya,” Kairišs says. “For me, it was immediately okay. I had to do it. But when we were looking for co-producers’ money, very often people were concerned about how it would look and if it would [seem like] a caricature or something. But I always said it sounds great. It’s a film about Ulya, and it’s not my idea. And I’m totally not interested in just a, let’s say, ‘normal’ or traditional film.”

Avots told THR earlier this year that, for him, Ulya felt like a story similar to Werner Herzog’s The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser. And his director had the same instinct. “My first impulse was that this is a little bit like a Werner Herzog film about a giant,” he shares.

Asked about other influences, the director mentions that he suggested that he and cinematographer Staroń watch Ingmar Bergman’s psychological drama Persona. “It’s probably an influence, or an influence on the aesthetic,” Kairišs acknowledges.

But the physical look and movements were mainly key to diving inside the person at the heart of the film. “My first major task for myself and the artistic team was how to go into her mind,” the filmmaker tells THR. “I was interested in showing the film from her inside right from the beginning. Of course, there are a lot of objective things, but I still found it important to show the invisible world of this human.”

As Avots told THR earlier in the year, Semjonova was a neighbor of his in Latvia’s capital, Riga. They developed a bond, and she trusted the team behind the film. The end of Ulya features a symbol of that bond: a photo of the athlete, who died in January, with Avots.

Focusing on one special person and her challenges and story helped make the film feel universal, the filmmaker believes. “While we were trying to go inside her head and make a very subjective film, it somehow also became a film about all of us – everybody who can identify with having an inner freak that we hold inside,” Kairišs offers. “Everybody has something that you want to hide that responds to all the standards that the modern world demands of you. You are somehow killing your darling, probably, your real authenticity, so the film is very universal.”

How does the director feel about Ulya representing Latvia in the international Oscar race? “It’s my third time,” he emphasizes. “You go to those Oscars with a small budget from Latvia, but the response to the film at screenings has always been amazing. And [premiering at] the Cannes festival was a dream for me.”

Kairišs also emphasizes the box-office success that Ulya has become back home. “In Latvia, it’s a real blockbuster,” reaching around 105,000 admissions and counting since its launch earlier this year, he says. That makes Ulya the most successful Latvian film in the country’s cinemas in 2026, putting it ahead of such Hollywood blockbusters as The Odyssey and Minions & Monsters. It is currently even the second most successful film of 2026 overall in Latvian cinemas, just behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Says its director: “It’s an unbelievable success for a black-and-white art house film.”

#723. Brandi Carlile, Leon Thomas & Magnus Ferrell Christmas Covers (Plus a JYT Original) Adorn Starbucks’ First Holiday Album in More Than a Decade

Coco Jones, TRÍADA & The Womack Sisters are also featured on Holiday Blend, which arrives today on streaming services & coffeehouse playlists.

For the first time in more than a decade, Starbucks is getting back into the holiday music business.

The new album Holiday Blend — featuring Christmas covers from Brandi Carlile, Leon Thomas, Coco Jones, Magnus Ferrell, TRÍADA and The Womack Sisters and a yuletide original from the boy band JYT — arrives Wednesday (Nov. 4) on streaming services and coffeehouse playlists via Interscope Records and Universal Music Group, Billboard can exclusively reveal.

The last time Starbucks put out a holiday album was Holidays Rule back in 2012, which featured The Shins, Fun., The Civil Wars, Paul McCartney and more.

For the new album, Carlile performs Joni Mitchell’s “River,” which starts with the holiday-set lyrics “It’s coming on Christmas/ They’re cutting down trees/ They’re putting up reindeer/ And singing songs of joy and peace.” Thomas gets us ready for a funky, festive holiday with his version of James Brown’s “Soulful Christmas.”

Ferrell — who covers the “Happy Holiday / The Holiday Season” medley released by Andy Williams in 1963 — says being part of Holiday Blend “felt like a chance to make something that’s both new and nostalgic. I grew up hearing these songs, so getting to record them in my own way was a pretty special experience.”

For her take on “It’s the Most Wonderful Time of the Year” — another 1963 Williams release — Jones said she “was honored and excited to put my own spin on such a beloved holiday classic, and I hope my version brings a little extra joy to people’s celebrations this season.”

The boy band JYT contributes the brand-new song “This Christmas” to Holiday Blend, and the quintet is “pumped” to be part of the Starbucks compilation. “The idea that someone could be ordering a Refresher and hear our song playing is actually crazy,” reads a statement from the group. (Sample lyric: “It’s just you on my wish list/ All I need is your peppermint kisses.”) “This Christmas” was written and produced by JYT mastermind Freddy Wexler, along with co-writer Elliah Heifetz and co-producer Gian Stone.

TRÍADA contribute the only Spanish-language song on the album, with their cover of Luis Miguel’s “Llegó La Navidad,” which itself is a spin on “Winter Wonderland.” “We hope this version feels familiar and fresh at the same time,” the Argentine trio says. “The song has such a beautiful feeling at its heart, and singing it in Spanish let us connect with it in our own way.”

Finally, The Womack Sisters serve up a Stevie Wonder classic, covering his 1967 hit “What Christmas Means to Me.” “For our family, Christmas is the best time of the year,” the R&B trio says. “The holidays are about togetherness, so singing ‘What Christmas Means to Me’ felt like a natural way to celebrate the season and share a piece of that family connection.”

Holiday Blend will also honor the season of giving by including a $500,000 donation to World Central Kitchen to support humanitarian relief efforts around the world.

“Music has always been part of the Starbucks experience, and we are building on that legacy in a way that feels fresh for today,” says Erin Silvoy, Starbucks’ senior vice president, global marketing & channel development. “Holiday Blend brings together incredible artists to put their own spin on songs we all know and love. My hope is that it becomes part of the soundtrack to the season, creating a little more joy and connection whether you’re in a Starbucks coffeehouse or wherever the holidays take you.”

Starbucks has a long history in music, starting with the acquisition of music retailer Hear Music in 1999 and continuing with exclusive music releases in partnership with Concord Music Group. Back in 2006, a Billboard article reported annual album sales of 3.6 million units or approximately $65 million in music revenue via Starbucks. In 2015, Starbucks coffee shops stopped selling CDs, but the brand has continued its music efforts, including a longstanding partnership with Spotify.

#722. Democrats Just Took the House and the Senate. Get Ready for a Whole Lot of Media Investigations.

David Ellison, Lachlan Murdoch, Mark Zuckerberg and other moguls are likely to find themselves facing inquiries, and perhaps hearings, over their deals and Trump ties.

In early February, just a few weeks before David Ellison’s Paramount secured its deal to pry Warner Bros. Dicovery from Netflix’s grasp, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and WBD chief revenue and strategy officer Bruce Campbell were hauled before Congress to defend their deal.

“I want to thank Mr. Sarandos and Mr. Campbell for coming here,” Sen. Cory Booker said in his opening remarks. “It is not fun often to testify before Congress. Sometimes I wonder if it ranks higher than a visit to the proctologist or to the dentist.”

What followed were tough, pointed, and sometimes overtly political questions, which Sarandos and Campbell had to navigate. Sen. Hawley, for example, accused Netflix of hosting content that “promotes a transgender ideology.”

Ellison had been invited, but declined, citing the fact that, after all, Paramount’s bid had been rejected by WBD.

The next Congress is unlikely to accept that answer.

Nor can he just ignore Congressional Democrats’ inquiries into his dealings, as he did last year.

With Democrats securing the House and the Senate in stunning fashion, the investigations into the Trump administration on Capitol Hill will begin. And there is reason to believe that the administration’s relationship with media companies, both positive and negative, will be among their top priorities. And yes, subpoenas may be in order.

Congress may not be able to block any deals they don’t like, but they can inflict pain through investigations and forced disclosures. And attention all CEOs: If Democrats in power get their wish, you should be prepared to testify.

A source working for one Democratic senator says that members of Congress in both houses are eager to haul executives in to ask about their deals and any rumored quid pro quos, with Skydance’s mega-deal for WBD and the ongoing Fox-Roku deal drawing particular scrutiny, as is the TikTok U.S. sale to Oracle, Silver Lake, and MGX.

Also of interest are the deals big tech companies like Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX have with the government for data centers, AI, and other services, and, yes, perhaps Amazon’s deal for the Melania Trump documentary, which its chairman Jeff Bezos framed as a “very wise business decision.”

Skydance’s move to raise cash from Middle East sovereign wealth funds and others like SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also of interest.

Booker made his intentions clear in a statement after Paramount’s settlement with the state AGs:

“This merger is the product of corruption hiding in plain sight. Secretary Hegseth stood in the Pentagon press room and said he couldn’t wait for the Ellisons to take over. Paramount was a constant presence at the Justice Department once it needed the deal pushed through. But when Congress asked questions, the company ignored our inquiries and refused invitations to testify. On the night of the shareholder vote, Ellison hosted a dinner honoring President Trump. Then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, the official responsible for approving this deal, was in attendance,” Booker wrote.

“This administration has turned merger review into a marketplace for political favors,” he continued. “That is why I will examine every merger this administration has approved, and why I will keep fighting to pass the CLEAN Mergers Act, so that no company can ever again buy its way past the law.”

At the same time, there is a desire to investigate what they see as overreach by the administration, particularly as it relates to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, which is in the process of attempting to strip Disney’s ABC of its local TV station licenses, and may be in a position to review NBC’s licenses shortly pending the NBCUniversal spinoff from Comcast. Anthropic’s feud with the DOJ may also come under scrutiny.

Any one of those deals could see the media companies brought before Congress to address their treatment by the administration, but also expose them to online attacks and revelatory details that they may prefer to avoid.

Just look at the child safety hearings held by Congress in 2024, where tech executives like Mark Zuckerberg, Evan Spiegel, Shou Xhew and Linda Yaccarino were put through the ringer (Zuckerberg memorably was asked to turn and apologize to families of victims of abuse).

The window for dealmakers to get major media, entertainment or tech deals through D.C. without that proverbial proctology exam may be nearing an end.

This is part of The Hollywood Reporter’s ongoing midterm coverage. You can check out all of the pieces here.

#721. 5 horror franchises that went to space... and one that absolutely should have but didn't
